slides.title: General Data Considerations
slides.teach: These are design tradeoffs. Learn why each factor matters rather than memorizing the words alone.

slides.title: Data States
slides.raw:
Data States
Data at Rest
Data in Transit
Data in Use
slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: Data has different security needs depending on whether it is at rest, in transit, or in use. At rest means stored, in transit means moving across networks, and in use means actively processed in memory/CPU.
course.why: A control that protects one state may not protect the others.
course.example: Disk encryption protects a database file at rest; TLS protects records in transit; access controls and protected execution help while data is in use.
course.exam: CompTIA often asks which control fits the data state. TLS/VPN = transit; disk/database encryption = rest.

slides.title: Data Sovereignty
slides.raw:
Data Sovereignty
Where data is stored
Where data is processed
slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: Data sovereignty means data is subject to the laws and jurisdiction of the location where it is stored or processed. Cloud replication can move data across borders without users realizing it.
course.why: Legal and contractual obligations may restrict where specific data can reside.
course.example: A company configures a cloud service so EU customer data remains in approved European regions.
course.exam: Location/jurisdiction restrictions = data sovereignty/residency. Geolocation can help identify or enforce location.

slides.title: Geolocation
slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: Geolocation identifies or uses the physical location of a user, device, or resource. It can support access policy, fraud detection, data-residency enforcement, and incident investigation.
course.why: Location is useful context but can be inaccurate or spoofed, so it should not be the only authentication factor.
course.example: A login from a country where the employee has never traveled triggers an additional authentication challenge.
course.exam: Impossible travel and unusual location are indicators; geographic restrictions can also enforce data or access policy.
